title: Until We Return — interactive work surfaces
provenance: Original OpenAI ImageGen paintings of seven interactive work surfaces. Native PNGs retain the generated bytes. coordinate_system: Percentages of the full uncropped 3:2 image. Point arrays are [x, y] measured from the upper left.

assets.caption: Sea chest in the salvage
assets.prompt: Surgical continuity edit of the first supplied 3:2 full-bleed painted game illustration, guided by the two detail references of the shut and open instance of the actual chest further away. This is ONE very close view of the CLOSED working tool chest from that same half-grounded 1864 schooner. The FIRST picture dictates the close workbench camera and the exact horizontal seam between lid and front: retain this horizontal joint and its small triangular chip at x73.5%, y60%, and the tight seam at x20%, y60%. Replace the first picture's uniform flat vertical strip at x38% with the actual period HINGED HASP of the other two references. The little basal plate is horizontally oriented, attached to the LID ABOVE the seam. Its vertical tongue swings down over the fixed front keeper on the box, with a small hole near its free rounded bottom, and has no padlock. Reddish brown forged wrought iron with charcoal and lighter worn edges. No second lock, no decorative pirate lock. Base plate and pivot around x38%,y48%; hanging tongue crosses x38%,y60%; its far tip near x38%,y76%. In the final close view the standing abraded face board and lid lip must be warm honey ochre adzed wood as in second image, subtle cool shadow bands, nails recessed as in this working chest. The old outer iron hoops in image 1 belong to a different chest; remove these and reveal the oak beneath; this new box has NO dark vertical metal edge bands. Slight bevel to the lip; preserve the distinctive little broken wedge of timber as the only legal pry place at x73.5% y60%. Show a little cool blurred sea in upper left as in the existing close camera. No cloth draped from above: the actual chest lid is bare golden wood in the supplied far view. North grey daylight from the left. An original highly considered maritime field sketch in opaque gouache and economical sepia pen, natural salt weathering rather than heavy pencil hatching. Preserve the first picture's exact full-bleed view of ONE nearly square-on face, not the zoomed-out views of the other reference photos. This is played by fitting a prybar under the dark notch to the RIGHT of the clasp, so give the shallow notch genuine depth at exactly x73.5 y60. NO bar, tool, block, hand, person, text, UI, watermarks, modern hardware, labels or measurement marks. Keep 1536x1024 3:2.

previous_revision.prompt:

Weathered wreck-salvaged chest, impression of wet cold dawn. The nearly horizontal lid seam is at y60% crossing x20 and strap at x38. No bar, added hardware, lifted lid or gaping joint.

open.prompt: Make the matching OPEN state of the FIRST attached close-up of this wooden castaways' tool chest. The entire image must have exactly the same fixed camera, foreground wood grain, front wall, nail heads, proportions and direct light as that close up. The second reference is the very same open chest seen zoomed out: its lid rotates up on its rear hinges (towards the sea), the long tongue of the hasp GOES UP WITH THE LID, and only a small, old iron keeper remains on the fixed front at x37%,y71%. The keeper is a little closed projecting iron staple on its riveted horizontal oval base, unmistakably separate and NO dangling strap below it. Reference 3 shows the correct old axe and tinderbox shapes. Make the lid fully unambiguously open: we see its inside near vertical around the rear of the box, cropped at the top of this close camera; its formerly frontward edge (carrying the tongue) is NOW HIGH UP and outside crop at the top if necessary. A yawn of physically correct interior shadow above the fixed front edge at y61% reveals a single modest iron-bladed hatchet with short turned wooden handle and a small tarnished old brass tinderbox half hidden beside it, a recognizable flint inside. They lie horizontally within the box well back inside the rim at y40–55%, not leaning on the front or protruding in the foreground. Limited reflected light on just these tools. NO extra implements. The triangle nick was a splinter in the LID; with the lid lifted the stationary top of the front wall has a narrow bevel and may have tiny wear. No floating dark wedge, pry bar, human hands, captions or overlay. Keep the entire LOWER 39% of the first image precisely registered wherever the hanging hasp was not covering it; same plank knots and nail positions. Do not change camera, zoom out, or rotate the box. Tight, cinematic front-on workbench view in the beautiful original gouache style, wide physical grain and ink details, salt-worn honey oak. Original 3:2 landscape 1536x1024.

fulcrum.prompt: Make ONE tiny close-up transparent cutout prop for a maritime gouache historical adventure game, a very short chunky rough-sawn wedge-shaped OAK FULCRUM BLOCK drawn as if propped against the upright side of a ship's chest in 1864 while a flat iron bar levers on its top edge. Oblong trapezoid foot, side face dark warm brown with two narrow visible old saw marks; end grain with small curved growth rings. Three-quarter front/left and slightly overhead view so one sees the flat chamfered top and two end faces. Flat on its lower edge, with the upper contact edge rising slightly towards the right, top takes iron bar. About a palm long and finger thick; the block is ~2.1 times wider than it is tall, not a cube. Good silhouette clear at only 45 pixels wide. Opaque broken warm gouache, fine sepia nib and sparse cool grey rubbed corners, lit from upper left, restrained warm oak and soft charcoal, 19th-century maritime field-notebook. Single object isolated on transparent alpha. No background, no floor, no cast drop shadow, no pile, no iron, no tools, no frame or type.
